rounds.proof_sketch: The kernel is launched with 1D block config: threads=256, so blockDim.x=256, blockDim.z=1. Original loop: 'for(i=tid; i<cols; i+=256)' — each thread handles stride-256 indices. Mutated loop: 'for(i=tid; i<cols; i+=1)' — each thread handles all indices from tid to cols-1. Both cover all indices 0..3999. Critical: all threads read from the SAME shared[] array after __syncthreads(), so every thread writes the SAME value shared[i] to output[row*cols+i]. The race conditions are benign — all writes to location i write shared[i].
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes blockDim.x (=256) to blockDim.z (=1) in the store loop stride. This causes each thread to iterate over all remaining indices instead of striding by 256. However, all threads share the same view of the shared[] array after the __syncthreads() following the scan computation. When multiple threads write to the same output index i, they all write the same value shared[i]. Since CUDA guarantees that writes of the same value to the same location produce deterministic results, the output is identical regardless of which thread(s) perform each write. The mutation creates massive redundant work but doesn't change the computed result.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation introduces benign race conditions where all racing threads write identical values. No value pattern can distinguish the outputs because the semantic computation (cumulative sum in shared memory) is unchanged, and the write-back phase preserves all correct values despite redundant writes.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing effectiveness, consider mutations that alter values being written rather than just write patterns. Benign race conditions (where all threads write identical values) are provably equivalent. EMD Layer 3 correctly identified this equivalence. Future static analysis could detect when a loop's stride change only affects redundancy, not correctness.
